sentences.text: The only known specimen of Juravenator is a juvenile individual measuring about 75 centimeters in length.
This animal was a small bipedal predator.
Its upper jaw featured four front teeth with serrations on the back edges, while the rest of the maxilla held eight additional teeth.
The middle section of the tail possessed unique bow-shaped joints known as zygapophyses.
Fossilized skin from the tail and lower hind leg shows normal dinosaur scales alongside traces of what may be simple feathers.
Small areas of the fossil preserve impressions or remains of soft tissues.
Researchers interpreted small round structures on the tail as integumentary sense organs similar to those of crocodiles, which would be the first such organs found in dinosaur skin.
Small rounded stones interpreted as ooids were found within the belly area of the Juravenator specimen.
The fossil was discovered during a 1998 paleontological expedition organized by the Jura-Museum Eichstätt at the Schamhaupten chalk quarry.
Near the end of planned excavations, two volunteers found a chalk slab showing clear remains of vertebrates, and initial preparation revealed the head of a small theropod.
The specimen was found in almost complete articulation, with only the skull, pelvic girdle, and front tail section partially disarticulated.
Juravenator starki was formally named and described in 2006 by Ursula Göhlich and Luis Chiappe.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Juravenator may have been nocturnal, though this might be due to the specimen being a juvenile.
Juravenator may have used these sensory organs to detect aquatic prey like fish while wading in water.

Fossils of isopods found with the specimen suggest they scavenged the carcass while it was floating, though researchers debated whether the isopods found with Juravenator scavenged the carcass or parasitized the living animal.
Juravenator was originally classified as a member of the family Compsognathidae.

Some studies classify Juravenator as a basal member of Maniraptora rather than a compsognathid, and a 2013 analysis classified Juravenator as a coelurosaur closely related to but not part of Compsognathidae, placing it near Ornitholestes outside Maniraptoriformes, while Juravenator belongs to the parent group Coelurosauria.

Juravenator lived approximately 152 to 151 million years ago in the Late Jurassic period in the Franconian Jura of Germany, living in what is now Germany during the Late Jurassic period, living approximately 150 million years ago during the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic, and lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, from 152.21 to 149.2 million years ago.
There is an ongoing debate regarding whether compsognathids belong within Maniraptora or represent a more primitive group.
